title: Designing an Elevator System
description: Explore scheduling algorithms like SCAN and LOOK, model elevator state machines, and coordinate multiple elevators with priority handling.

segments.text: Every building you walk into has elevators. But have you ever wondered what algorithm decides which elevator answers your call? Let's design one from scratch.
Our system needs to handle multiple elevators, multiple floors, up and down requests, door open and close, and priority calls like fire emergencies.
The simplest approach? First Come First Served. Process requests in order. But imagine an elevator on floor one going to ten, then back to two, then to nine. Wildly inefficient.

Enter the SCAN algorithm. The elevator moves in one direction, servicing all requests along the way, then reverses. Like a disk head sweep. This is why it is called the elevator algorithm in OS textbooks.
LOOK is smarter than SCAN. Instead of going all the way to the top or bottom floor, it reverses as soon as there are no more requests in the current direction. Less wasted travel.

segments.thought_prompt: If you have three elevators and a request comes from floor 7, how do you decide which elevator to send?

segments.text: Each elevator is a state machine. States include idle, moving up, moving down, door opening, and door closing. Transitions are triggered by requests, arrival at floors, and timeouts.

The dispatcher is the brain. When a hall call arrives, it evaluates every elevator's current position, direction, and load. It picks the one with minimum cost, often based on estimated time of arrival.
Priority handling is critical. Fire mode overrides everything, sending a designated elevator to the ground floor. VIP floors get weighted priority. Emergency stop halts the car immediately.
Our class design: an Elevator class with state and floor queue, a Request class for hall and cabin calls, a Dispatcher that assigns requests, and a Building that holds everything together.
Before we wrap up, consider this.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you handle the scenario where all elevators are full and a new request comes in?

segments.text: Elevator design teaches you state machines, scheduling trade-offs, and real-time coordination. These patterns appear everywhere, from thread schedulers to network packet routing. Master the elevator, and you have mastered a universal pattern.
